text:
Not as a 100% allocation. A single S&P 500 fund is a reasonable core holding, but it shouldn't be all of it at 56.

The main risk is sequence-of-returns: a large drop in the years just before or after you start withdrawing does permanent damage, because you sell shares at low prices to fund living expenses. The S&P 500 fell about 49% in 2000-02 and about 57% in 2007-09, and the 2000s decade returned roughly nothing in nominal terms. At 56, a 50% drop leaves little time to recover before you need the money. The index is also concentrated: the top 10 holdings are around a third or more of it, mostly large tech, and it is all US.

The case for it holds if most of your retirement spending will be covered by a pension, Social Security, or other income, so this money can sit untouched for 15-30+ years, and you would hold through a 50% drop without selling. If you'd sell in a crash, the allocation is wrong for you regardless of expected return.

A common alternative is something like 60-80% stocks, with the stock portion diversified beyond the S&P 500 (total US or global), and the rest in bonds or cash covering several years of withdrawals. A 2035-2040 target-date fund holds roughly that mix at your age.

What would change this: a retirement date 10+ years out, large guaranteed income, and a track record of staying invested through a downturn would make a high equity share (still probably not 100%) defensible. Also, if the money is in a taxable account, selling current holdings to move into the fund can trigger capital gains tax, so check that first. In a 401(k) or IRA, switching has no tax cost.
